PNG supports four prediction methods: Sub (predicts from the left neighbor, best for horizontal gradients), Up (predicts from the pixel above, best for vertical gradients), Average (predicts from the average of left and above pixels), and Paeth (smartly picks between left, above, or diagonal). Each row in a PNG image can use a different prediction method, and PNG encoders try each method per row and select the one that compresses best. This approach works because adjacent pixels in images are usually very similar to each other.

questions.lessonContent: LZ77 is the second trick in PNG's lossless compression pipeline, used to find and replace repeated patterns with compact back-references. When LZ77 spots a repeating pattern, instead of storing the same sequence twice, it says 'go back X values and copy Y' - this tiny reference is much smaller than repeating the values. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data, and any pattern within that window can be referenced instead of being repeated. This technique is particularly effective for images with large solid color regions or smooth gradients where the same values appear frequently.

Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently (like 0 appearing 60% of the time gets just 1 bit) while using longer codes for rare values. Finally, all this compressed data gets wrapped in the PNG format with headers and checksums for integrity verification.

questions.lessonContent: Images appear smooth and continuous, but they are actually composed of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers representing the amount of red, green, and blue to mix together, with each value ranging from 0 (no color) to 255 (maximum intensity). questions.lessonTitle: The Two Fundamental Approaches to Image Compression
questions.lessonContent: There are two core approaches to compressing image files. The first approach involves throwing away parts of the image that humans won't notice, which is called lossy compression. The second approach involves being clever about how you store every pixel while still reducing file size, which is called lossless compression. These two ideas power common file formats like JPEG and PNG, as well as ZIP files, web traffic, and most of the internet. Lossy compression cannot restore the original pixels once discarded, while lossless compression preserves every single pixel perfectly.

The second concept uses references to point back to repeated patterns already seen in the data rather than storing them again. The third concept assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently, similar to how Morse code uses short signals for common letters like 'E' and longer signals for rare letters like 'Q'. Together, these techniques allow images to be compressed significantly while maintaining quality.
